items.body: Across its seventeen tracks, Wahj brings together electronics, industrial textures, processed strings, Arabic vocal traditions and fractured rhythms in combinations that keep changing shape. Individual elements remain recognisable without settling into familiar forms, while images of voice, disappearance, radiance and return recur throughout the album. Wahj took shape over five years, and the events of that period inevitably entered the music. As Toni Geitani explains in the accompanying interview, the album was not initially conceived as a meditation on collapse. The idea emerged gradually as the circumstances surrounding its composition changed. Collapse here is not a single catastrophic moment. Ruin exists alongside what persists, with Geitani attentive to the lives and voices that political violence can obscure. This runs through the lyrics as well as the music. Voices appear and disappear, sometimes sounding like invocations, sometimes carrying fragments of collective memory. On the brief “Sawtuka”, Geitani repeats, “Raise your voice higher and higher. Even if they bind you, even if they take you through death, the echo of your voice will remain forever.” The refrain turns persistence itself into an act of resistance. “2092” projects the idea into an imagined future in which “every fascist has fallen, and their glory belongs to nothingness,” before asking, “Does love remain when everything has vanished?” “Hal”, “Ruwaydan Ruwaydan” and the extended instrumental closer “Madda Mudadda” draw on ritual, repetition and moments of ecstatic release, with their meanings left open. The title, Wahj, points towards radiance, although Geitani gives the word no easy redemptive meaning. Light appears amid destruction, sometimes faintly, and does not cancel what surrounds it. In “Tuyoor”, the image is carried by birds: “The birds flying above you do not belong to the ruler who oppressed you. They watch the sky, not the earth beneath you.” The image opens a space outside the authority of the ruler, even while that authority continues to shape life below. Throughout Wahj, Geitani keeps returning to such spaces: voices that outlast attempts to silence them, traces of love after disappearance, and forms of life that continue amid devastation. To discuss the making of Wahj, we approched Toni Geitani directly. Wahj is described as an album about collapse, but one that refuses to remain trapped within its concept. Across the record, images of ruin, mourning, exile, and disappearance are constantly accompanied by gestures toward radiance, return, and endurance. How did you approach balancing these opposing forces while writing the album? I didn’t start working on the album with any intention of a “theme”, in this case collapse. I also wasn’t trying to narrow down the album to one thematic focus. It was an intuitive process that mostly guided the work. But it is true that as the project developed over five years, a lot of horrific events unfolded; consecutively and sometimes simultaneously. This naturally affected the relation to my work in a way that pushed me into ending up with these tracks, which I could eventually describe as being about collapse. By saying that the album refuses to be reduced to collapse, I’m intentionally pushing back against the idea that collapse is only a sudden, singular catastrophe. I was born in the 1990s in post-civil-war Lebanon, so from early on I was surrounded by war stories told by family and friends. After continuous exposure to these stories throughout my life, I came to understand that they were not stories of the past only, but of a collapse that kept resurfacing in different forms. At the same time, however, I was also exposed to another image of collapse that dominated global media and felt especially present in my teens in the 2000s. It was that of an image imported from the West, romanticized, and flattened into spectacle. It also ignores how, for some populations, collapse is already ongoing rather than a problem of the future or an isolated incident that can be inherited and prolonged. That difference matters to me because, for many of us, imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism are not warnings of an apocalypse to come, but they morph to become ongoing and almost fixed conditions. So when I was writing Wahj, I didn’t feel that I was trying to balance opposing forces simply because I do not see them as opposing, but inevitably coexisting. Instead, I was trying to remain faithful to everything catastrophe-centered narratives tend to erase: memory, resistance, regeneration, and the human capacity to continue. They are what must be reclaimed from within it. The lyrics repeatedly return to voices, echoes, and acts of calling out across distance. In “Sawtuka” (“Your Voice”), for example, the refrain insists that a voice survives even imprisonment or death, while tracks like “2092” and “Tuyoor” are structured around questions of who is listening and who remains absent. What role does the voice play in Wahj—as memory, resistance, testimony, or something else entirely? For this album, I composed the music before writing the lyrics. I would often record a vocal melody, sometimes with words that made sense and sometimes not, simply to find a fitting flow and have it as a placeholder until the final vocal recording. But before I began writing and recording the lyrics, the genocide in Gaza began alongside the war on Lebanon in 2023, so I stopped working on the album because I felt uneasy about prioritizing it. At that point, nothing made sense anymore. But somehow, by the beginning of 2025, I found the motivation to finish the project, and thus the lyrics were written. In my opinion, the voice can hold many roles at once, including the ones mentioned in the question. It is not intended to be a tool for meaning-making, but rather a presence moving through space, carrying the emotional and political conditions of that space with it. However, its position is immanent rather than observational. It does not stand outside the world to explain it. Instead, it emerges from within that world and continually reaches outward, while refusing to die. The lyrics inevitably reflect the experience of witnessing a 24/7 livestreamed ongoing Palestinian genocide, and the rage, injustice, betrayal, pain, and constant aggression we have been dealing with for many years. However, I do not wish to limit the album’s interpretation to the events of the past three years. As I mentioned earlier, collapse is not a one-time event or a singular fall, but I insist that it emerges from an ongoing oppression imposed on us by the same death machine. Musically, the album moves between processed classical instruments, layālī-inspired vocal passages, industrial textures, dark ambient atmospheres, and fractured electronic rhythms without ever fully settling into any one genre. Did you begin with a clear sonic vision for Wahj, or did this hybrid language emerge gradually during the five years of recording between 2021 and 2025? I did begin with a fairly clear sonic vision for Wahj, in the sense that from the beginning I wanted it to explore different genres and subgenres while still remaining rooted in electronics. What emerged gradually was not that intention itself, but the specific language the album took on through time, collaboration, experimentation, and everything that happened across those years. After releasing my first album in 2018, I wanted to keep exploring and collaborating before putting out another record. Between 2018 and 2020, I performed many live shows in Lebanon, where improvisation became an important space for testing new ideas and compositions. Over time, this left me with more than a hundred sketches, from which I selected the ones that felt less attached to a single genre and more committed to a shared atmosphere and universe, even if that universe itself remains unstable and fluctuating. When I began my studies at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam in 2021, that process expanded further. Being surrounded by many different kinds of musicians pushed me to explore classical instrumentation, processing, and different digital approaches in ways I had not tried beforehand. I recorded many phrases and ideas with musicians there, often without knowing exactly what their final form would be, because part of the process was discovering how their playing could be transformed and absorbed into the album’s sonic world. In that sense, the hybrid language of the record was both intended and gradually revealed. As mentioned earlier, I returned to working on the album in the beginning of 2025, and that final period inevitably shaped the work in a profound way. So while the album’s sonic foundation was there from the beginning, its final form was shaped by a long process of experimentation, disruption, and response to the world it was being made within. Several tracks evoke futures rather than simply documenting the present. The title “2092,” in particular, imagines a distant horizon where “every fascist has fallen and their glory belongs to nothingness,” while love and memory continue to endure. What attracted you to speculative or future-oriented thinking as a way of responding to contemporary political realities? I would like to make a distinction between futurism as typically understood through a Eurocentric lens which is rooted in Euro-American frameworks and historically entangled with imperialism and fascism – and counterfuturism that emerged from the Global South which functions to complicate normalized notions of time and technology rather than projecting a single vision of the future. And this is precisely what I intend to convey in the practice of imagining futures in the album, which attempt to articulate a cultural politics of time and become a means of writing alternative histories that distance themselves from any established history already written. This could mean reclaiming the right to think beyond imperialist scripts through collective knowledge, agency, and world-making rather than celebrating rupture, domination, or heroic modernity. In other words, I’m trying to open possibilities from within collapse, and thus, this framework differs from futurism as an approach for technocratic future-thinking. For example in “2092”, I try to treat the future as a tool to ask whose futures have been denied or flattened, instead of assuming it operates in a single path of progress. The political visions I sing about are not predictions, but they gesture toward an intense need to imagine the aftermath of collapse in the hope that something promising might emerge from it. That being said, I don’t intend for my songs to be frontal or overly obvious in their interpretation, and I welcome listeners to bring different meanings to them. You wrote a master’s thesis titled Sampling as a Political Medium, examining questions of power, appropriation, and cultural memory. Wahj incorporates repurposed regional sounds and references while constructing an entirely new sonic language. How has your thinking about sampling evolved since that research, and how do those ideas inform the album’s relationship to Arabic musical traditions and collective memory? My thinking on sampling has certainly evolved, although I do not see it as a linear progression that concluded with my thesis. The research was conducted alongside the creation of the album and I continue to work with samples, therefore I am always interacting with this topic. Throughout Wahj, I work with both political and non-political samples that either have a political or non-political intention. For example, samples from my personal life, my urban surroundings, and of traditional instruments, the choice is more nuanced because it’s integrated and processed within the soundscape and ambient textures. However, for samples that are more frontal and forward, like the sampling of Amal Dunqul’s poem, “Spartacus’ Last Words” in “Madda Mudadda” the intention is more clearly deliberate and explicit. These choices are bound to spill into collective memory, as I am borrowing sounds from my surroundings and heritage. Take the sample of Lebanese singers Sabah, Wadih El Safi, and Walid Gholmieh in “Wasla”; I was drawn to their voices for reasons I can’t quite articulate. But the moment I tried fitting the sample into the track, it felt seamless. My sampling choices are meant to re-activate archive sound, and insert these historical moments into the present to let them speak again through a different context. All voice samples from the album come from televised interviews, and I chose them not only for their raw, untampered sound, but also because they carry something of the world they were recorded in. To sample them is to pull them back into light and reactivate voices forced to be erased for new audiences, while also making visible the power structures that determine whose memory is preserved and who is erased from the record. Ultimately, these sampling choices are always, in some way, in conversation with the cultural memory I carry, bringing the historical in contact with the contemporary. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — In 1971, Biblical themes and rock operas were all the rage. This was David's contribution to the phenomenon. Though recorded in LA with a 38-piece orchestra (including bassist Carol Kaye, keyboard specialist Don Randi, and guitarist Mike Deasy), the lead vocalists are only listed as the singing group "The Dillons" while David's friend Julian "Cannonball" Adderley politely serves as the album's producer.A1. "Overture" (5:49) the first half is bombastic symphony orchestra, very well composed and rendered--like an overture. At the 2:45 mark there is a stoppage which is slowly filled by wah-wah-electric guitar, electric bass, funk-rock drumming, and dirty/raunchy electric piano as the orchestra horns and strings re-engage, only in more of a support/accent role--though their melodic presentation is continuous of those melodies presented in the opening half. Very cool! Very solid and well-rendered and powerful. (9.5/10)A2. "Comfort Ye My People" (2:45) Elton John-like solo piano opens this before male tenor voice enters to sing the words of the song's title. I really like this arrangement, the way David builds around Ed Dillon's singing and then start to increase in intensity and dramatic effect. (9.125/10)A3. "And The Glory Of The Lord" (4:50) like a rock-orchestra arrangement of a gospel choir rendering of this liturgical song. The vocal arrangements are quite rich and sophisticated; the rock instrumentation a little out of place. (9/10)A4. "Behold" (2:35) led by a Black female Gospel-Blues singer (a Dillon?), acoustic guitar is the only support instrument for the first minute--the first verse. Slow development brings in blues-rock instrumentation with orchestral horn support. Carol Kaye's bass and the electric piano are the most prominent of the rock musicians. Nothing very special or even dramatic here. (8.75/10) B1. "Pastoral Symphony" (5:35) layers of strings open this one, presenting the melody in a kind of fugue before more sections of the orchestra are slowly brought in. This sounds a bit like a New Age "spreading out" of a Pachelbel song. Nice but, again, nothing ground-breaking or exceptional. (8.75/10) B2. "And The Angel Said Unto Them" (2:52) opening with the same orchestral strings, in the second half of the first minute the music eventually gives way to a R&B combo for a Black female soprano gospel singer to sing over. The full orchestra is quite present, serving as thick and integral support, though the drums, bass, electric piano, and electric guitar work are the most active and aggressive here--especially in the song's second half--as anything else on the album. (Could that have been Earl Palmer on the drums?) (9/10) B3. "Glory To God" (3:03) elements of both female and male choirs are presented as opposed, woven, and antiphonal/echoing parts of the lyrical presentation while gentle funk-rock band and full symphonic orchestra participate from start to near-the finish. Quite a disciplined performance that David got out of these singers (as well as the orchestra). (9.125/10)B4. "Hallelujah" (3:23) we all know and love it. This one sounds like a slightly slowed-down, BARRY WHITE-version of the tune--until, that is, the second minute when the music moves into an all-instrumental section where Don, Mike, and the orchestra's horn section are given a little room to express themselves in solos. But then we return to the horn-embellished vocal delivery. I have to admit that I've heard many versions of this "song" that I like far better. (8.75/10)B5. "Worthy Is The Lamb" (2:52) nice Gospel choir music with totally-unnecessary and unfulfilling rock instrumentation. Even the orchestral work on this one feels as if it "gets in the way" of the fine vocal work. "The Dillons" are definitely a fine choir. (8.875/10)Total time: 32:40I have to say that this was one of the few times that I actually thought that the great Carol Kaye's bass playing was unbefitting to the music, which feels really weird since I revere her work and instincts so highly. Where I think David's work--his "Rock Interpretation"--started really strongly, I think it went off the rails somewhere in the middle of the Second Side. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of the fusion of rock, jazz, R&B, and classical musical styles.

Paradoxically, this is a notably superior effort yet the 2 tracks on which she sings are among the weaker entries, not bad at all like the inane "Pass it on" but not nearly the equals of the authentic charms of the TIR NA NOG like ballad "Sometimes"; the lively spiritual endeavor of "Waves upon the ether", the sheer charm of "Whispering Ned", and the jaw dropping prog folk exuberance of "Kalyope Driver", their best by far to this point. The Anglo-Celtic flourishes are better integrated than on the debut even if they insist on weightlessly superficial 30 second interludes. A bonus cut on "An Evening with Dando Shaft" does suggest better things ahead with Ms. Bolton and indeed she may well have helped more than mere credits and front line contributions might imply. As you are discovering this unjustly suppressed talented collective along with me, I can only add that time will tell as we pivot freely through history from our advantage point.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — In the early 2000s, Savatage's core members were juggling their time and musical ideas between the band and the increasingly demanding side project Trans-Siberian Orchestra, created by Jon Oliva, producer Paul O'Neill, and arranger and keyboardist Robert Kinkel. It was against this hectic backdrop that the American band released "Poets and Madmen" (2001), their eleventh album, whose central theme revolves around a loose adaptation inspired by the tragic fate of Kevin Carter, the photographer who captured the harrowing image of a Sudanese child crouching on the ground, watched from a short distance by a vultur - a photograph that earned him the Pulitzer Prize in 1994.The album features the return of Oliva's raw and expressive voice as lead singer, a greater prominence of Chris Caffery's rhythmic and heavy guitar riffs, and a solid instrumental foundation, supported by Kinkel's symphonic arrangements. All of this lends, on the one hand, that combination of theatrical stage presence and razor-sharp energy characteristic of metal outbursts in tracks like the anguished "Stay with Me a While", the martial "Commissar," and, above all, the epic "Morphine Child", an elaborate and highly fluid epic that includes superb choral segments and is surely the jewel of the album.On the other hand, there's room to revisit the genre's raw, primal roots with the fast-paced, '80s-style heavy track "Drive"; the density of doom metal with Sabbath-esque touches in "I Seek Power" - another great track - ; and the pasty "Awaken," with Oliva on the verge of vocal breakdown. There are also some acoustic subtleties in hybrid tracks like "The Rumour (Jesus)" and "Man on the Mirror", where the band navigates peaceful valleys and abrupt instrumental mood shifts with great skill.The self-indulgent and theatrical "Got to Get Back to a Reason" - a track that attempts to capture the emotion in the air and give the album an epic, redemptive ending - ends up also being the final piece in the band's discography. Because, despite the musicians' intention to maintain both projects simultaneously, their packed schedules and commitments made their coexistence unsustainable. After the album's promotional tour and in the absence of an official statement, Savatage went on a "hiatus" that has now lasted 25 years...3.5/4 stars

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — D'Arcansiel, an Italian band with a French comically misspelled name (all the more strange given that the opening track of their 1988 debut album is aptly titled "Un Arc dans le Ciel"), which emerged in the mid-1980s and disbanded a few years later, we were familiar with their three neo-prog albums (including the quite respectable *Still Searching*, released in 1990), heavily influenced by Marillion from the same era, though none of them left a lasting impression on our minds, already saturated with prog masterpieces of all kinds. Suffice it to say, I wouldn't have bet much on a new Arcansiel album ? I would have been wrong, because that's exactly what just happened with *Hard Times*, an undeniable success in a very personal RPI style that easily makes you forget the band's earlier efforts. This proves once again, as the saying goes, that it's never too late to do things right. "Too Late!" Yet this is the painful cry of alarm delivered?through the voice of the excellent singer Marco Leccese and the band's new keyboardist Davide Sorella?right from the introduction of the first track, a nearly 18-minute suite that Sorella wrote and composed.The state of Planet Earth is cause for concern, and even if it's not certain that the point of no return has been reached, we can safely say that we will not leave this place in the same condition we found it. The beauty of the world is fragile, and humankind is a malevolent shadow that has never ceased to wither it away. Progress continues its rapid march regardless of the circumstances and seems to defy even the most alarming signs. So is it too late to avert disaster? Sorella tells us instead that it's too late to keep wasting our time making bad decisions or failing to take any serious action.Musically, "Too Late" is a grand symphonic prog epic as captivating and inexhaustible as the theme it explores. With a neo-Baroque-inspired leitmotif that gives center stage to a keyboard-dominated instrumental section (a commanding synth, a very assertive piano, a mischievous harpsichord, and a swift Hammond organ playing in rondo form), all in service of hyper-melodic vocal parts?reminiscent of what Oliviero Lacagnina has recently done with The Samurai of Prog, or even Gryphon at their most prog?this majestic epic manages to bathe discreetly in a fluid, slightly jazzy atmosphere, then bursts into a symphony that is more melancholic than desperate, at times bordering on the tragic. After such a fireworks display?18 minutes that seem to fly by in the blink of an eye and that one wishes could last an eternity?the rest might seem to take a back seat, less grandiose. But this impression quickly fades upon listening to the next three tracks, which are just as brilliant."Hard Times" (like the title of Dickens' novel), can be understood as "Difficult Times" but 'Hard' also means "Tough." We are indeed living in an era with problems that are difficult (but not impossible?) to solve on every level (social, cultural, ethical, ecological, political?); but we are also in a world that is hard to live in for many of us?and that "us" encompasses the majority of living beings. Arcansiel's album offers us some enlightening accounts of this. From the scathing and mocking "Puppets and Puppeteers" (a description of one of the most irritating aspects of new media) to the disillusioned "Heaven Is Not Here" (beware of smooth talkers and false promises), the social issues addressed in *Hard Times* are critical reflections that remain relevant and never fail to move the listener.The result of a collaboration between bassist Felice Lombardo and guitarist Sebastiano Valvo, "Puppets and Puppeteers " (7:51) brings a fairly distinct shift in musical atmosphere by adopting a deliberate tempo with irregular measures in a powerful neo-prog style reminiscent of early Asgard (Leccese's vocals play a part in this), illuminated by dazzling synth solos that readily give way to a magnificent lyrical guitar solo. "Heaven Is Not Here" (11:22), written by the bassist, also offers remarkable moments, especially for those who appreciate Jon Anderson's more peaceful work paired with Genesis's "Supper's Ready."Personally, I have a soft spot for the unpredictable "My Old Same Mistakes" (7:27), written by the duo Sorella and Valvo in a melodic style quite similar to the romantic, post-Gabriel era of Genesis, and in which Marco Leccese once again works wonders (his "Save Me," sung with great conviction, is sure to be memorable), though the second half?following a medieval-influenced instrumental bridge?leans toward a swaying jazz-rock style, before concluding with Canterbury-style prog, all seamlessly strung together. As surprising as it is delightful.More than 30 years have passed since *Still Searching*, and only drummer Gianni Lavagno remains to ensure the band's continuity and the legitimacy of the Arcansiel name, though he did not participate in writing the songs for *Hard Times*. The compositions penned by the other three musicians?evolving into a sort of shimmering neo-prog with a distinctly Italian sensibility, featuring numerous twists, breaks, and inspired resurgences?are far richer and more diverse than those of the original Arcansiel. Reusing the same name may seem like a questionable choice, even an abuse of the name. But after all, the label on the bottle isn't very important when it contains such nectar?to be savored without moderation to make our lives sweeter.

items.body: Review by Rysiek P. — An opportunity like this certainly cannot be overlooked. Twenty years after releasing their debut album, *Armed Forces of Simantipak*, the band Khatsaturjan?whose name derives from the renowned Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian?has released a new record titled *Monolog Chronosa*. Their discography also includes two other albums - *Disconcerto Grosso* (2010) and *Beast, Machine & Man* (2015) - and their history is notable for the fact that, as early as their 2002 debut single *Aramsome Sums*, they performed their own "rock" versions of Modest Mussorgsky's *Night on Bald Mountain* and Hector Berlioz's *March to the Scaffold*. All of this was presented in progressive hard-rock arrangements that incorporated elements reminiscent of the band Gentle Giant. Furthermore, critics hailed the group's first album as a benchmark for symphonic rock. One might pessimistically remark, "But that was years ago". Yet, it is certainly worth checking out where Khatsaturjan stands today. The band's latest release comprises forty-seven minutes of music spread across seven tracks, with an album title suggesting that the passage of time is the central theme. This phenomenon is observed and described from various perspectives - including, perhaps most importantly, the human condition and the personal, often highly subjective experience of life passing by. The title of the opening track - "Lessons (On Human Obsolescence)" - gives one food for thought right from the start. However, do not expect dark, atmospheric arrangements here. The composition is remarkably balanced,almost conservative in its playing style and employs familiar progressive rock tropes, with one notable exception: a strong emphasis on vocal polyphony (a true hallmark of this album) and a more prominent role for keyboards. These two elements define the musical structure of the song, which opens with the sound of a bell before embarking on a progressive journey rich in engaging tempo shifts and instrumental virtuosity. The second track, "What Was True," takes a slightly different approach. Here, the band clearly leans toward a modern progressive sound, successfully utilizing "new textures" to craft a unique atmosphere that straddles the line between atmospheric progressive rock (or even neo-prog) and a vocal-harmony-driven ballad. Once again, vocal polyphony and synthesizers serve as the building blocks for both this specific track and the album as a whole. The track "The Dystopian Spirit Of Club Energy" also features a piano-and-synthesizer-driven sound. Yet, in this composition, the band draws upon classical music and classical time signatures. The piano sets the arrangement's course, serving as a backdrop for highly impressive vocal performances. Only halfway through does the track remind us that it is 2026, showing how a guitar-driven rhythmic boost can yield a truly successful result. Incorporating electronic elements into the arrangement only enhances the musical value of this piece, which runs over five minutes in length. It was only while listening to "Song Of Days" that I realized what truly draws me to the band's music: a delicacy and almost theatrical storytelling style, skillfully blended with classical influences, alongside magnificent tales sung with a masterful, gradual build-up of vocal intensity. With a full arsenal of musical tools at their disposal, Khatsaturjan selects only those that fit the symphonic-progressive narrative, all while keeping classical music traditions close at hand. "Song Of Days" is a perfect example of this approach. It makes brilliant use of symphonic arrangements, blending them with flawless vocal lines and weaving in thoroughly modern progressive guitar motifs to create a truly well-crafted track. "DID Memoir" shares a similar, song-oriented character. It opens with a "classic" sense of grandeur, progressive guitar work, and... such delicate vocals. Everything weaves together into a structure that challenges the listener - filled with improvisational passages that hark back to classical music and, as an added bonus, theatrical farce-style interludes appearing midway through the fourth minute. Just listen closely around the five-minute mark for a dose of rap; this element, yet another instance of the piece's stylistic multiplicity, is entirely justified given the title: "DID Memoir." While the acronym refers to Dissociative Identity Disorder, it also serves as a fitting title for the track's eclectic, multi-stylistic nature. Following a symphonic opening, the penultimate track on this magnificent album - "The Keepers of the Philosopher's Stone" - simply sends shivers down the spine with its superb vocal lines. It features backing vocals, humming passages, and a lead vocal that stands out tonally, its rough timbre lending an air of deep mystery. Yet, what makes this composition truly exceptional is the extensive and successful incorporation of motifs drawn from classical music; the violin sounds and classical time signatures transform this five-plus-minute piece into a remarkable puzzle of motifs and an intricate arrangement. A madrigal-like character, blended with thoroughly modern synthesizer and guitar sounds, seems to elevate the track's central theme - fittingly so for a song about the "Philosopher's Stone," which here truly transmutes individual notes into "gold." With this release, the end comes all too soon. Were it not for the fact that the closing track - "Mundus Meus (This World of Mine)" - employs every possible device to captivate the listener from the very first note, one might feel that the magnificent preceding track left something musically unresolved, a void that could neither be filled nor replaced. "Mundus Meus..." stands as a magnificent anthem and the perfect culmination of the album; the Latin lyrics sound both prophetic and majestic without detracting from the depth of the message. And although the track features numerous gentle prog-metal solos, it remains, at its core, a thoroughly symphonic-progressive composition. If I say that I am very - truly very - pleasantly surprised by the latest work from the group Khatsaturjan, is that recommendation enough? If not, I'll add that the band features essentially the same lineup as on their debut and subsequent albums, even though musical light-years have passed since that first release (in 2002). Atte Kurri (vocals, bass, keyboards), Ilkka Piispala (vocals, drums, keyboards, bass), and Ilkka Saarikivi (vocals, keyboards, bass, violin) continue to demonstrate that musical trends don't matter to them. It is significant that Khatsaturjan is a group of friends who get together only when they want to record something; they are not a band that makes a living from touring and recording albums. On their Facebook page, the band writes: "We work slowly because Khatsaturjan is not our profession - it is a passion project and a beloved hobby. Whenever we decide to work on a new album, we know a years-long effort lies ahead, with no financial reward whatsoever. Yet, time and again, we take on new projects." Perhaps this approach allows them to maintain a sense of detachment and find the tranquility needed to create new music? You surely know that things tend to flow more easily when there are no deadlines hanging over your head. And since we will likely have to wait a long time for the next sign of musical life from Khatsaturjan, we should simply enjoy this highly successful release - one that has earned a spot in my top ten albums of the year.

items.body: These two releases from Anna Fedorova and András Schiff both feature Brahms’ late Opp. 117–119 sets, but Schiff’s also includes Opp. 76 and 116. The most interesting distinction, though, is the choice of instrument: Schiff plays a Blüthner built around 1859. Amazon Presto Apple Amazon Presto Apple Fedorova’s Op. 117 is best defined by her exquisite voice leading, present in each of the three works. In faithfully maintaining the integrity and continuity of the thematic material, she creates a fluid and expansive quality despite the structural minimalism. The melodiousness also elicits different but equally comforting emotions throughout: empathy in the Andante moderato (track 1), gentle yearning in the Andante non troppo (track 2), and gravity in the Andante con moto (track 3). Schiff’s performance is equally effective but in a different manner: the period instrument, while resonant, has a lighter profile than Fedorova’s. This evokes a Classical elegance that we don’t always associate with late Brahms. His Andante moderato from Op. 117 (Disc 2, track 1) expresses a more coy tenderness. The Andante non troppo (Disc 2, track 2) has an even greater degree of fragility and transparency than Fedorova’s. The final piece sounds more subdued and solemn, although the beautiful shimmer of the middle section is not to be overlooked. Op. 118 introduces more distinct personalities throughout, all of which Fedorova faithfully captures. The opening Intermezzo (track 4) may not be as bold or rhapsodic as the reading from Francesco Piemontesi that I reviewed recently, but it is meaningful and contemplative. The A major Intermezzo (track 5) is exquisite, considerably more intimate than I’ve heard elsewhere, and tells of her impressive palette of softer dynamics. The G minor Ballade has a satisfying austerity, which she draws from the full bass register of the piano. The final Intermezzo (track 9) stands out as it convincingly juxtaposes two divergent personalities: a quietness characterized by enigmatic undertones and a drama bolstered by the undulating accompanimental material. Schiff’s Op. 118 opens with a grand, emphatic reading of the first Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 4) that also underscores Brahms’ colorful chromatic complexity. The A major (Disc 2, track 5) is less introverted but instead takes on a brisker tempo that reveals a grazioso profile. I expected his G minor Ballade to move a little faster than Fedorova’s, but it feels even more deliberate and measured; the major middle section, while largely calm, possesses an intriguing undercurrent of suspense thanks to the Blüthner’s lower register, which growls ever so subtly. The F minor Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 7) again carries a Classical undertone that feels almost Schubertian in its refined approach. With the exception of the heroic finale, Op. 119 contains some of Brahms’ most introspective writing. While Fedorova’s B minor Intermezzo (track 10) brings this out, I found the E minor (track 11) surprisingly vibrant and highly responsive to harmonic twists and turns. The C major is quite placid—perhaps too much so; it might benefit from more perkiness and forward movement, as we hear in Richard Goode’s recording. Fedorova’s E-flat Rhapsody, though, proves a most satisfying end to an excellent set: it is full of authority and reminds us of the composer’s signature symphonic profile. If only the recorded dynamics didn’t sound as though they were reaching their limits. In the louder passages here and elsewhere, there is a slight distortion that can be picked up even at low volume. András Schiff (left, photo © Nadia F. Romanini) and Anna Fedorova. Schiff brings out the intricate details of Brahms’ compositional style in his Op. 119. The E minor Intermezzo (Disc 2, track 11) gets off to a slow start, but a patient listen reveals how the pianist makes pointed distinctions between staccato and legato interchanges. His C major Intermezzo flows a bit better than Fedorova’s and gives off a uniquely ballet-like feel. The finale, too, possesses a distinct personality: Schiff purposefully rests on certain beats, creating a particular “gait” that helps emphasize the work’s substantiality. Nearly 15 years separate Op. 76 and Op. 116, and Schiff’s performances reveal the differences between the two. Op. 76 essentially marks the start of Brahms’ late period, but the pianist introduces a more restless, youthful energy, especially in the active passages. The pieces are more loosely connected given their eclectic characters, and he spotlights this individuality in the stark differences between the timidly playful B minor Capriccio (Disc 1, track 3) and its C-sharp minor counterpart (Disc 1, track 6), which is much more stubborn and off-kilter. Op. 116, compositionally more unified, is where we hear Schiff at his most powerful, rousing, and authoritative. The stormy D minor Capriccio (Disc 1, track 16) or the fierce final moments of the last work are perfect examples. Although Schiff offers a slightly wider scope of offerings, both performances are equally compelling and enjoyable—yet undeniably distinct to each musician. Fedorova’s readings evoke the depth and spirituality of Brahms’ late period, while Schiff’s puts an interesting Classical spin on certain works without losing their introspective essence. items.body: The Cult released their fifth studio album, “Ceremony,” on 23 September 1991, through Beggars Banquet in the United Kingdom and Sire in the United States. The English rock band, who had started the decade before as the post-punk groups Southern Death Cult and Death Cult, made the record as a two-piece with session players. It turns 35 this year. By the time the sessions began, the touring line-up had gone. Bassist Jamie Stewart retired and moved to Canada after the final leg of the “Sonic Temple” tour in April 1990, and drummer Matt Sorum left to join Guns N’ Roses, leaving vocalist Ian Astbury and guitarist Billy Duffy as the only official members. Todd Hoffman played bass and James Kottak drums on the demos. For the album itself, Mickey Curry returned on drums after his session work on “Sonic Temple,” with Charley Drayton on bass. Richie Zito produced, with Astbury and Duffy co-producing, and also contributed keyboards and harmonium. Benmont Tench played organ, piano and mellotron, Scott Thurston added synthesizer and piano to “If,” Suzie Katayama played cello on “Indian,” and Alex Acuña handled percussion on “Indian” and “Wonderland.” Tommy Funderburk sang backing vocals across most of the record, joined by Donny Gerrard, Mona Lisa and Yvonne St. James on “Sweet Salvation.” Phil Kaffel engineered, Mike Fraser mixed, and George Marino mastered the album at Sterling Sound in New York. Pre-production ran at Oliver Ferrand Studio in Los Angeles and Mates in North Hollywood, with recording at Music Grinder Studios in Hollywood and recording and mixing at A&M Recording Studios. The eleven tracks run 63 minutes and 38 seconds: “Ceremony,” “Wild Hearted Son,” “Earth Mofo,” “White,” “If,” “Full Tilt,” “Heart of Soul,” “Bangkok Rain,” “Indian,” “Sweet Salvation” and “Wonderland.” Astbury and Duffy wrote all of them. “Wild Hearted Son” opens with an excerpt from “The Grass Dance” performed by The American Indian Dance Theatre, and “White” quotes Lawrence Lipton’s 1959 book “The Holy Barbarians,” which Astbury took as the name of his next band in 1996. “Wild Hearted Son” was the first single, followed by “Heart of Soul” in 1992. “White” appeared as a single in Canada only, “Sweet Salvation” was issued in Argentina in 1992 as “Dulce Salvación,” and the title track came out as a promotional single in Spain. The cover photograph, taken by John Running, drew a lawsuit. The parents of the Native American boy pictured on the sleeve sued over the unauthorised use of their son’s image, a case Entertainment Weekly reported on 19 June 1992. The New York proceedings against Warner Bros. Records were dismissed in February 1997 for lack of personal jurisdiction; a separate action filed in the District Court of South Dakota on 10 April 1995 was terminated on 16 May 1995. The dispute held up the record’s release in several territories, with South Korea and Thailand not seeing it until 1992 and Turkey not until the band played Istanbul in June 1993. Alan Forbes handled the art direction and design with the band. “Ceremony” reached number 9 on the UK albums chart, was certified gold by the BPI, and went platinum in Canada. Sources differ on its US peak: Wikipedia’s entry on the album gives number 25 on the Billboard 200, while its entry on the band gives number 34. The Ceremonial Stomp tour took the record through Europe in 1991 and North America in 1992, with Michael Lee on drums, Kinley “Barney” Wolfe on bass and John Sinclair on keyboards. The album streams on Spotify. About The Cult Ian Astbury formed Southern Death Cult in Bradford, Yorkshire, in 1981, with guitarist Buzz Burrows, bassist Barry Jepson and drummer Aki Nawaz Qureshi. They played their first show at the Queen’s Hall in Bradford on 29 October 1981, signed to Situation Two, an offshoot of Beggars Banquet, and released the triple A-side single “Moya” in 1982 before ending after sixteen months with a final Manchester show in February 1983. Jepson went on to co-found Into A Circle with Paul “Bee” Hampshire in 1985. In April 1983 Astbury teamed up with Billy Duffy, who had played in the Nosebleeds alongside Morrissey, then Lonesome No More and Theatre of Hate. The new band, Death Cult, added bassist Jamie Stewart and drummer Raymond Taylor Smith, later known as Ray Mondo, both from the London post-punk group Ritual. Death Cult debuted live in Oslo on 25 July 1983 and released the “Death Cult” EP the same month, with the “Gods Zoo” single following in October. Nigel Preston, previously of Sex Gang Children, replaced Mondo that September. The group shortened its name to The Cult in January 1984, ahead of an appearance on the Channel 4 programme The Tube. “Dreamtime,” recorded at Rockfield Studios in Monmouth with producer John Brand, arrived in September 1984 and reached number 21 in the UK. Preston was dismissed in June 1985 and Big Country’s Mark Brzezicki played the “Love” sessions that July and August; the Steve Brown-produced album reached number 4. Les Warner drummed on the world tour that ran from late September 1985 to June 1986. The follow-up was first recorded as “Peace” with Brown at the Manor Studios in Oxfordshire, then re-cut in New York with Rick Rubin and issued in April 1987 as “Electric,” which also reached number 4. Kid Chaos joined on bass for that tour, with Stewart moving to rhythm guitar. “Sonic Temple,” produced by Bob Rock and recorded in Vancouver between October and December 1988, followed in April 1989 and went gold in the UK and platinum in the US. After “Ceremony,” Astbury and Duffy replaced the touring band in 1993 with Craig Adams of The Mission and drummer Scott Garrett, the line-up that recorded “The Cult” with Bob Rock in October 1994. The band split in March 1995 during a South American tour. Astbury formed Holy Barbarians, whose only album “Cream” came out in May 1996, and released the solo record “Spirit\Light\Speed” in June 2000. Duffy worked with Coloursound alongside Craig Adams and Mike Peters, then Dead Men Walking and Cardboard Vampyres. The Cult reformed in 1999 with Sorum and bassist Martyn LeNoble, signed to Atlantic for “Beyond Good and Evil” in 2001, and went on ice again in late 2002. Astbury spent that second break fronting the surviving members of The Doors in a group billed variously as The Doors of the 21st Century, D21c and Riders on the Storm. He announced his departure in February 2007, stating: “I have decided to move on and focus on my own music and legacy.” The Cult had already reunited in January 2006 with drummer John Tempesta, guitarist Mike Dimkich and bassist Chris Wyse. “Born into This,” produced by Martin “Youth” Glover of Killing Joke, came out on Roadrunner on 16 October 2007. Cooking Vinyl signed the band in May 2011 and released “Choice of Weapon” on 22 May 2012 and “Hidden City” on 5 February 2016, both produced by Rock. James Stevenson replaced Dimkich on rhythm guitar in 2013 and Grant Fitzpatrick replaced Wyse on bass in 2015. Duffy also appeared on Wayne Hussey’s 2020 charity remake of “Tower of Strength,” alongside members of Depeche Mode, The Smiths, The Mission, Gary Numan, etc.. The band signed to Black Hill Records in May 2020, began recording at Rockfield in August 2020 with producer Tom Dalgety, and released “Under the Midnight Sun” on 7 October 2022 with Charlie Jones on bass. On 23 October 2025 the group announced a touring hiatus of undetermined length to concentrate on writing and recording. “Ceremony,” the only album in that catalogue made without a settled line-up, turns 35 this year.

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: https://dunkelheitprod.bandcamp.com/track/ajna-transmissions

items.body: Adrian Utley, the guitarist and co-founder of Portishead, has reworked “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” from Polish composer Mariusz Szypura’s “Chopin Residue,” a project that removes the piano entirely from nine of Frédéric Chopin’s best-known piano pieces. The rework arrives today as the latest single from the double album, which Cleopatra Records brings to CD and double vinyl on 16 October; an immersive Blu-ray edition mixed in Dolby Atmos is already available. Chopin Residue by Mariusz Szypura Szypura said working with Utley was a long-held ambition: “Adrian and Portishead are among my favourite musicians. The sound, the approach to making music, the search for unobvious and lo-fi textures, all of it had an enormous influence on me.” Szypura kept the harmonic structure and phrasing of Chopin’s originals while stripping out the instrument itself. He described the decision as a matter of respect rather than provocation: “I rejected the piano immediately. […] I decided Chopin didn’t deserve such profanation. I could only approach this material through the prism of my own sensitivity, harmony, and deconstruction. So I took the piano out. […] The piano was the delivery system, not the content.” Adrian Utley’s rework of ‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ “Chopin Residue” splits into two discs: “Deconstructions,” on which Szypura rebuilds nine Chopin pieces with a cast including Lee Ranaldo (Sonic Youth), David Pajo (Slint), Joey Waronker, Gail Ann Dorsey, John McEntire (Tortoise) and John Stanier (Battles), and “Reworks,” on which a second group of artists takes those deconstructed recordings further from the source. Utley’s “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” opens the second disc alongside reworks by Fennesz, Matthew Herbert, Masayoshi Fujita, Sean O’Hagan, Jim O’Rourke, Christine Ott, Benoît Pioulard and Abul Mogard. Szypura described the difference between the two discs directly: “‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ is Adrian’s reconstruction, not my piece with his guitar on top. That is the principle of the whole second disc: nine artists, nine rebuilds, each in their own language.” The two discs are designed to be played together as well as separately, an idea that extends into the Blu-ray edition’s Dolby Atmos mix. Szypura said: “They were built to overlap. […] In stereo you hear an arrangement. In Atmos you’re inside the harmonic space with the piano missing from the middle of it. […] That’s not a format upgrade, it’s closer to what the piece was always trying to do.” “Chopin Residue” gets its UK stage premiere at London’s Cadogan Hall on 26 September, as part of the Polish Jazz Festival. Its packaging has also picked up a Bronze A’ Design Award and a Red Dot Award. About Adrian Utley and Mariusz Szypura Adrian Utley was born in Northampton in 1957 and moved to Bristol in the mid-1980s, where he played guitar in touring bands led by jazz organist Big John Patton and drummer Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. He co-founded Portishead in Bristol in 1991 with Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, co-producing and playing on the band’s albums “Dummy” (1994), “Portishead” (1997) and “Third” (2008). Outside the band, Utley has recorded and toured with Marianne Faithfull, Jeff Beck and Will Gregory of Goldfrapp, leads his own ensemble Adrian Utley’s Guitar Orchestra, and has scored film and audio work with director Nic Roeg, naturalist David Attenborough and Britain’s National Trust. Mariusz Szypura is a composer, producer and visual artist born in 1972 and based in Warsaw. He started out in the early 1990s in the Poznań rock band Happy Pills before founding his main recording project, Silver Rocket, releasing five albums including “Infinity Fidelity,” a Dolby Atmos record that won Gold for Music/Film Cover at the 2025 European Design Awards. His installation work includes “in:human” at the Centre for Contemporary Art Ujazdowski Castle in Warsaw (2024) and “êkhos” at Lincoln Center during Unsound Festival New York (2024). “Chopin Residue” grew out of that installation practice: Szypura first released the album digitally and on 2LP, 2CD, 2MC and Blu-ray through his own Black Element Label in Warsaw on 28 November 2025, alongside gallery and listening events in New York, Osaka, Los Angeles and Warsaw. Cleopatra Records now extends that release internationally, bringing “Chopin Residue” to CD and double vinyl on 16 October 2026 while the Blu-ray Immersive Edition remains available from its earlier release.

items.body: Sandie Trash announces the single “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Debris (Métal Urbain) and Richard Belgium (MI6), the first track revealed from the upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” The French post-punk and new wave project has not confirmed a release date for the album itself, and “Poupée Panik” is not yet available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page, Instagram or Facebook. Sandie Trash builds ‘Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka’ around the Motel Dakota The nine-track album is set around a recurring fictional location, Room 17 of the Motel Dakota, with several tracks written as character pieces tied to that setting: “La perversita,” “Poupée Panik,” “Élégance déplacée,” “Gloria Dakota” and “Sophie qui aime les avions.” Sandie Trash describes the record as a “sabotage” of eighties nostalgia rather than a nostalgic homage to the decade. Alongside Eric Debris and Richard Belgium, the album credits a wide cast of guest contributors: Emmanuelle 5 (Dead Sexy), Olivier de Joie (Les Fils de Joie), Max Freeth (Ausgang), Karbokroma, Kelsey Warren (Blak Emoji), Jérôme Lefdup (Lefdup & Lefdup), Gilles Le Guen (Denner) and Oli Le Baron (Ici Paris). One track, “I Trash You Fuck Off,” is credited with a guest vocal from Helno, the former Lucrate Milk member who went on to front Les Négresses Vertes until his death in January 1993. Sandie Trash’s announcement does not explain how that vocal appears on a track dated 2026, whether as a sample, an archival recording or another arrangement, and no further detail was available to confirm it. Eric Debris also mixed and mastered the album at ATX Mastering studio. The cover art is by Italian illustrator Volt.B. About Sandie Trash Sandie Trash is a French punk and electro project based in Périgueux, fronted by the singer of the same name and built, album after album, around a rotating cast of guest musicians on individual tracks. The approach dates back at least to 2018, when the project’s “Le French Peep Show” paired a new musician with each song on the record. On Bandcamp, Sandie Trash’s confirmed discography includes the album “Outrageous brune,” released 25 February 2010 through Indies.Music.Productions with vocals from Sandie Trash and Maudd and mixing and mastering by Emmanuel Borie, and the 14-track compilation “Rose chewing-gun & Machine-gum (2006-2017),” released 29 May 2025 and gathering tracks and features from that decade, including contributions from Kloot Per W, Romeo Praly, Kim Ohio Fuzz, Marcel Vanthilt and Nina Courson. “Poupée Panik” and the album built around it, “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka,” continue that same collaborative format on a larger scale, bringing in musicians tied to Métal Urbain, MI6, Ausgang, Denner and other underground post-punk and EBM circles for a post-punk and new wave record set inside the fictional Motel Dakota.

items.body: Fawning, we’re brighter, we’re cautious, Falling like fighters, we’re caustic. Cracked up like actors, we’re lying. Daydreams and nightmares. Sharing cigarettes and leather trousers can feel like a promising start to eternity, until eternity begins to resemble an argument neither person can leave. Berlin’s Night Nail take that unhappy prospect to the dance floor on Vile Train, a gothic rock seduction in which two lovers become so absorbed in each other that escape begins to seem as impossible as happiness. The attraction is considerable; so is the damage. The song previews Infinite Fountain, Night Nail’s fourth studio album, due November 6, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Its accompanying video reunites the band with director and editor Jean De Oliviera, whose previous collaborations include Hollow Day, Little Armenia, and Narcoleptic Dream Catcher. Vile Train begins with a noise suspended somewhere between a buzz and a screech, while cold guitar tones gather around it with considerable menace. The drums establish their footing before a heavier, sustained riff saws through the opening, its melody making the abrasion strangely inviting. Around the thirty-second mark, the bass enters with a deep, brooding groove, and the guitar shifts into a lower, more resonant register. That change gives the song a mournful richness, setting the scene for Brandon Robert’s dark, swaggering delivery. Repeating synth figures tighten the tension beneath his voice, and roughly a minute in, the chorus sends the arrangement into a more urgent gothic dance beat. The construction is remarkably assured: each entrance increases the pressure, while the bass keeps enough melodic independence to make the groove feel alive. By the three-minute mark, its intricate phrasing has become a hook in its own right, moving beneath Robert’s breathy repetition of “Daydreams and nightmares” as a feminine voice echoes the words in whispers. The song’s pleasure comes from those relationships between the instruments, the way an ominous opening develops into something so physically persuasive. Robert found the initial inspiration during a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested a romance with a particularly poor prognosis. In the song’s conception, two dreamers inhabit separate modern realities until their fantasies bring them together. They exchange clothes, cigarettes, and intimacies, gradually making a prison of the connection that first seemed to offer freedom. Robert describes the result as “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The lyrics give that deterioration a nasty intimacy. Caution sits beside fawning, attraction beside aggression, and the lovers seem increasingly aware of the roles they have been playing. “Some days I wish I was her” carries the confusion further, towards the point where wanting another person begins to erase the distinction between their identity and your own. Against the recurring admission of lies, the fantasy of America offers another possible elsewhere. Every imagined exit seems to lead back to the same two people. Vile Train was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. That combination serves a song whose writing and arrangement make its gothic excess feel earned, with a chorus capable of turning private misery into a crowded dance floor. Directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera, the video gives Vile Train a stark black-and-white treatment, cutting between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor shots framed by stone arches and fountain basins. Black leather, dark glasses, and severe makeup give the pair a suitably funereal glamour, while tight shots of fingers on strings bring the song’s instrumental interplay into focus. Robert’s face repeatedly fills the frame, his dark lipstick and pale features isolated against the black background. Grain, scratches, and superimposed silhouettes of reaching hands disturb that severe simplicity, spreading across faces and instruments until the musicians seem caught behind the image itself. Robert’s own gestures towards the lens make the camera feel uncomfortably close, turning performance into something between an invitation and an accusation. The recurring close-ups and grasping hands give the song’s obsession a physical form, suggesting an intimacy that has become impossible to escape. It is an effective visual rendering of what the band calls the “afterlife of relationship hell,” where the desire to hold someone close has acquired a distinctly claustrophobic meaning. Watch the video for Vile Train below: Formed in Los Angeles in 2013, Night Nail relocated to Berlin in 2018, the year their debut album LA Demons appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed through Cold Transmission in 2020, with Fates Explained arriving on Metropolis Records in 2023. The archival release Early Demons and Demos and remix album Fates Remade followed in 2024. Their earlier work with producer Pete Burns of Kill Shelter helped establish a catalogue that connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes. Infinite Fountain also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the album with shows across the US, UK, and Europe during 2026–2027. In the meantime, explore their back catalog on Bandcamp.
