items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. items.body: 2026.09.23 デビュー20周年を迎え、ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全5曲に挑む新倉瞳さん。なぜ今、ベートーヴェンなのか？ 7歳でチェロと出会ったきっかけから、音楽家として大切にしていること、憧れの音楽家、新しいジャンルへの挑戦まで……新倉さんの音楽人生と「今」が見えてくる50の質問を前後編でお届けします。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る デビュー20周年の節目にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲に挑む 1. デビュー20周年おめでとうございます！ 20年前の自分に、今の新倉さんから一言かけるとしたら、何と言いますか？ 新倉 「安心していいよ」と言いたいです。自分が思っている自分と、他人から見える自分には、どうしても差があります。100人の人がいたら、100通りの自分の見え方があると思うんです。 20年前は「こうでなければいけない」とすごく気にしていました。でも今は、みんなが思ってくださった自分が自分でしかないと思えるようになりました。自分が思っていることを、意外とちゃんと見てくださっている方々もいらっしゃるので、そういったところでリラックスして、安心して楽しんでいればいいよ、と言いたいですね。 新倉瞳（にいくら・ひとみ） 桐朋学園大学音楽学部を首席で卒業し、皇居桃華楽堂新人演奏会に出演して御前演奏を行う。その後スイスに渡り、バーゼル音楽院ソリストコース・教職課程の両修士課程を最高点で修了。これまでに毛利伯郎、堤剛、トーマス・デメンガ、マーティン・ツェラー（バロック・チェロ）の各氏に師事。国内外で数多くの賞を受賞し、2017年に第18回ホテルオークラ音楽賞、2020年度に第19回齋藤秀雄メモリアル基金賞チェロ部門を受賞。桐朋学園大学在学中にEMI Music Japanより『鳥の歌』でCDデビューし、同レーベルから3枚、アールアンフィニからは『11月の夜想曲～委嘱作品集』を含む4枚のソロアルバムをリリース。ほかにも多数のアルバムを発表している。 かつてカメラータ・チューリッヒのソロ首席チェリストとして活躍し、スイスを拠点にヨーロッパや中央アジア、日本でもソリストや室内楽奏者として幅広く活動する。近年はクレズマー音楽や民族音楽にも造詣を深め、音楽祭に招かれワークショップやレクチャーコンサートも行う。カザフスタンの民俗楽器ドンブラも演奏し、2025年にはカザフスタン国営放送で日本人として異例の紹介を受けた。 使用楽器は宗次コレクションより貸与のマッテオ・ゴフリラー（1710年製）。2026年にデビュー20周年を迎えた。 2. 20周年の節目として、12月3日に俳優の南沢奈央さんの語りとともにベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを舞台のように届ける演奏会「ベートーヴェンの小径」を開催されます。まず、ベートーヴェンを取り上げようと思った理由を教えてください。どんな演出になるのでしょうか？ 新倉 私はいろんなジャンルの音楽に興味を持って活動してきましたが、20周年ということで、いわゆる「ザ・クラシック」みたいなプログラムに取り組みたいという思いもありました。これまで民俗音楽にも多く取り組んできましたが、ベートーヴェンの作品も紐解いていくと、民俗音楽との関連が見えてきます。だからこそ、節目の年にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲を取り上げるのは、すごくいいのではないかと思いました。 さらに、私のデビュー20周年の次の年がベートーヴェンの没後200年なので、長い期間で、お祭りみたいにできるかなと思った次第です。 演出については、当日までのお楽しみです。ただ、音楽をいわゆる舞台の主役にして、チェロ・ソナタが本編となって、語りの部分が幕間をつないでいくような感じにしたいと思っています。 3. 「ベートーヴェンの小径」では、演奏だけでなく構成・脚本・演出も手がけられます。なぜこのような舞台形式でベートーヴェンを届けたいと思われたのでしょうか？ 新倉 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを改めて勉強して、ベートーヴェンの生きてきた背景や彼が残した言葉などいろいろなものをリサーチしていくうちに、ものすごく面白いと思ったんです。そして、演奏で伝えることが使命ではありますが、せっかくだったら物語を交えてみるのはどうかな、と思いました。 南沢奈央さんとは、以前『罪と罰』という舞台でご一緒したことがあって、そのときも音楽が物語に介入していくような演出でした。南沢さんとその後ご飯に行ったときに、彼女も今年がデビュー20周年だと知り、「じゃあ何か一緒にやれたらいいね」と言って別れたんです。 その帰り道に、もし彼女にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタでご一緒していただけるんだったら、そういった物語を本当に組み込めるかもしれないと思いついて。いろんな点と点が、ピーンとつながったんです。 もうひとつの拠点、スイスで、著名な音楽家の方が演奏曲の背景をさらっとお話ししてからコンサートをするのを見て、すごく勉強になったんです。「こういうひと言があると入っていきやすいな」と。だから、演出とか脚本という言葉にするとすごくドラマティックですが、自然な流れなんじゃないかなと思っています。総合プロデュースとして、作曲家と曲の魅力や、自分が思っていることをお伝えできるきっかけになるんじゃないかなと思っています。 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央「ベートーヴェンの小径」 4. ベートーヴェンの5曲のチェロ・ソナタの中で、今のご自身に一番近いと感じる作品はどれですか？ 新倉 今の自分に一番近いと感じるのは、もしかしたら3番かもしれません。 私は、そのときに取り組んでいる曲が一番大事だと思うタイプ。でも、ベートーヴェンの5曲のソナタをそれぞれ見ていくと、1番と2番はベートーヴェン自身がピアノを弾いていたこともあって、ピアノが主役で、チェロはオブリガートのような役割なんですね。 それに対して第3番は、ベートーヴェンがいわゆるチェロ・ソナタとして舞台に乗せることを意識して作っているので、第1番、第2番とは全然違うんです。第4番、第5番になると、さらに即興的な要素も入ってきます。 そう考えると、自分が演奏家として人前に出るという意味では、第3番が一つのきっかけのような存在なのかなと思います。ロマンティックな部分もすごくあって、ロマン派への入り口にもなっていますし。 ただ、ベートーヴェン自身がソナタに対していろいろなアプローチをしていったように、私自身も変化していくと思うんです。だから、数年後には「やっぱり第5番かな」と言っているかもしれません。 初めてチェロを弾いたときに「もっといい音を出したい」と思った 5. チェロを始めたきっかけを教えてください。 新倉 もともと母がピアニストで、お腹の中にいるときからピアノを聴いていました。自然ななりゆきで母からピアノを教わっていたんですが、普段は優しい母なのに、ピアノの前では急に角がはえてきて（笑）。それで、だんだんピアノが怖くなってしまいました。 当時、父の仕事の関係でドイツに住んでいたこともあって、音楽がいろんな方とのコミュニケーションのツールになるということは、よく感じていました。音楽自体はもちろん大好きだったけど、ピアノを弾くことが怖くなってしまった私を見かねて、7歳くらいのときに母がドイツのトーンハレというライン川のほとりにある劇場に、よくコンサートに連れて行ってくれました。 母は、ピアノでなくてもハープやフルートといった女性が構えて美しい楽器を趣味でいいから演奏してくれたらといいなと思っていたらしいんです。でも、その頃オーケストラや室内楽を聴いて、「チェロって、すごく支えているのに主役にもなれるし、いろんな面があって、何より音色がきれいで、いい楽器だな」と思って、母に「あれがやりたい」と言ったんです。 そのとき母は、「足を開く楽器を選んだ！」と思ってびっくりしたらしいんですけど、8歳の誕生日にチェロがやってきました。 7歳にしてチェロに魅了されたという新倉さん 6. 初めてチェロを弾いたとき、どんな印象を持ちましたか？ 新倉 もちろん、体に当たって音が響くことには「わー」と感動しました。 でも、まだ小さかったのでフルサイズではなくて1/2サイズの子ども用のチェロだったんです。大人の演奏で聴いていたよりも、「あれ、なんか音があんまりよくない？」と思って。「もっといい音を出したい」と思いました。思っている音色じゃない、というのはすごく覚えています。当時から早くフルサイズになりたいと思っていました。 7. 子どもの頃、一番好きだったチェロの曲は何ですか？ 新倉 今思うと、ヴィヴァルディのチェロ・ソナタ第5番ですね。 わりと小さいときに取り組んだ曲だったんです。ヴィヴァルディの《四季》がすごく好きだったので、「チェロでもヴィヴァルディが弾けるんだ！」というところで、子どもの頃から好きでした。チェロを始めて1、2年後、わりと早い段階で取り組んでいました。 ヴィヴァルディ：チェロ・ソナタ第5番第1楽章 8. 「音楽家になろう」と決めたのは、いつ頃でしたか？ 新倉 中学生のときです。ピアノがちょっと怖くなって以降、チェロに関してはものすごく自由に、練習したいときに練習して、ほかの習い事も並行していました。クラシックバレエ、水泳、テニス、塾など、いろいろさせてもらっていたんです。 中学生のときには、絵描きや美術の道に進むことにも憧れがあって、どちらにしても芸術なんですけれども、少し悩んでいました。そんなときに、パブロ・カザルスの国連でのスピーチで、「わたしの故郷カタルーニャの鳥はピース、ピースと鳴くのです」とおっしゃっているのを聞いて、「どうして人間は争っているんだ」と思ったんです。 それはいまだに消えないテーマなんですけど、「音楽がそういった平和にちゃんと響くことができるんだ」と思って、絶対に音楽家になろうと思いました。 クレズマー音楽との出会いによって「優等生」から解放 9. 音楽家になっていなかったら、何になりたかったですか？ 新倉 絵描きに憧れがありました。薄い色を重ねる水彩画は苦手で、はっきりとした、わりとおどろおどろしい絵を描いていました（笑）。 10. これまでの音楽人生で、ご自身が大きく変わったと感じた出来事は？ 新倉 いまだに真面目気質ではあるんですけれども、今はだいぶ「不真面目になること」に、いい意味で慣れるようになったなと思っています。 大学生のときにデビューして、優等生でいないといけないという時期もありましたが、スイスで東ヨーロッパのクレズマー音楽に出会って、プロもアマチュアもいるバンドに参加するようになったんです。そこで、「優等生である必要ないな」と思って。音楽が好きで集まって、みんなで弾いている気持ちって、すごく大事だなと思うようになりました。 そこからすごく気持ちが落ち着いて、そうすると、キャリアもなぜか追いついてきたというか。クレズマー音楽に出会って、自分が「優等生でいなくちゃいけない」という意識がなくなったときに、すごく解放されたなと思います。 クレズマー音楽も収録したアルバム『魂柱と鞴』 11. もしチェロ以外の楽器をマスターできるとしたら、何を選びますか？ 新倉 実は2つあって、1つは昔から打楽器が大好きなんです。リズムってやっぱりすごいなというイメージがあります。今も趣味でサンバヘギというサンバの太鼓を叩いています。実は音楽之友社さんの前からスタートする神楽坂のパレードで、何回か叩いたことがあります。 あとは歌ですね。自分の声が楽器というのは憧れがあります。それができないから、チェロで歌を表現している部分があるのかなと思います。 歌は自分が楽器だから、それがダイレクトに伝わると思うんです。でも、それって生まれ持ったものもあると思うので、私は次はもっとカラオケでバリバリ歌える声質で生まれてきたいなと思います。 2025年「化け猫フェスティバル」より 編集部員にとっておなじみの会社周辺の光景に新倉さんが打楽器を演奏する姿が……！ 動画は新倉瞳さんのInstagramで！ 大切にしているのは「一音入魂」 12. 新倉さんにとって、チェロの一番好きなところはどこですか？ 新倉 歌を表現できるところです！ 13. 一番の思い出の曲は？ 新倉 エルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。取り組んでいた中学生のときに、祖父が亡くなったんです。私にとって初めての大好きな人の旅立ちだったので、人間の魂というものが音に乗るという経験を初めてしました。叫びきれない思いをチェロに乗せて叫べた、そういった経験ができました。 14. 生涯でチェロ協奏曲を1曲しか弾けないとしたら、どの作品を選びますか？ 新倉 これもエルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。高校受験のときにも取り組みましたが、エルガーはとても深みがあるので、大人になってから取り組むというイメージがあったんですけれど、ドロドロした絵を描くタイプだったからこそ、その深い音楽にシンパシーを感じていたのかもしれません。 新倉さんによるエルガー：チェロ協奏曲 15. 演奏するときに、一番大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 「一音入魂」です。一音一音、そこに何か意味がある音を出したいと思っています。 なんとなく音符を追うのではなく、「作曲家はどうしてこの音を残して、私はどのようにそれを汲み取ったらよいのだろう」とすり合わせて、音に魂を込めたいなと思っています。 16. 練習中など壁にぶつかったときはどうやって乗り越えますか？ 新倉 結局、ひたすら納得いくまで練習するしかないなと思います。私は悩みをそのままにしておけないタイプなので、悩みきることのほうが気持ちいいんです。ぶつかっていきますね。 練習したくない気分のときは、あまり悩まないで、やめて、ご飯を食べに行くなど気分転換して、また向き合います。 本番前のルーティンはなし！ 17. 本番前は緊張するタイプですか？ 新倉 準備が整っていると、あまりしないかな。もうやるしかないと思っているから。逆に、練習中のほうが「これ、間違えたらどうしよう」と緊張することもあります。そういうことを練習中に考えて、本番前は「ここまでやったから、もう大丈夫だろう」と思って挑みます。 18. 本番前に必ずすること、ルーティンはありますか？ 新倉 あまり決めないほうがいいと思っています。日本のコンサートホールのように楽屋がきちんとある環境ばかりではなく、海外の教会で寒い日にいきなり弾かなければならないこともある。そうすると、ルーティンを決めていて、それができなかったときに焦ってしまうんじゃないかなと思うんです。 なので、練習を始めるときは曲をパッと弾いて、弾けなかったところが自分のウィークポイントだと思うようにしています。 19. 「今日はいい演奏ができた」と感じるのは、どんなときですか？ 新倉 結局、自分にはどうしても厳しくなってしまうので、共演者やお客さまがいい顔、いい表情をしていたら「よかったのかな」と思えます。自分基準ではあまり判断できないので、ほかの人がいい顔をしているかどうかで「よかったのかな」と思えます。 ちなみにスタイルキープの秘訣は「服のサイズを変えないこと」だそう！ 20. 今、一番弾いていて楽しい作曲家は誰ですか？ 新倉 今はベートーヴェンです。常に変わっているんですが、今はベートーヴェンに改めて取り組んでいて、新しい発見がたくさんあります。 以前に聴いたときとは、やっぱり自分が変わっている。特にベートーヴェンは、私が幼少期に聴いてきた演奏は、どちらかというとロマンティックな演奏が多かったんです。 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ1番、2番は、チェロがオブリガート的な役目だと先ほどお話ししましたが、それでもチェロがリッチに演奏されることが今まですごく多かった。 でも、今改めて勉強し直してみると、ピアノとチェロの対話が面白いんです。例えば、チェロから始まるフレーズだと思って弾いていた部分が、改めて見るとピアノから呼応する形で出てきているんだな、と。そう考えると、「もっとさらっと弾いてよかったんだな」と思ったり。自分なりの解釈がはっきりしてきたというのが、楽しいです。 21. これまでに「この人の音楽はすごい！」と衝撃を受けた音楽家はいますか？ 新倉 1人ではないんですが、あえて1人選ばせていただくなら、堤剛先生です。堤先生の音って、どの曲を聴いてもわかるんです。 私とは違う解釈で演奏されていても、ショパンやリヒャルト・シュトラウスのチェロ・ソナタ、ドヴォルザークの協奏曲、バッハなど、先生の説得力のある音が今でも耳に残っています。音色だけでなく、生徒としてではなく、常に一人の芸術家として接してくださったことも大きいです。 私が自分に自信をなくしていたときには「あなたの実力でここまで来ている」と背中を押してくださったり、クレズマー音楽など新しいことにも「素晴らしいですね」と耳を傾けてくださったり。学生時代には、クラシックではない民族音楽のCDをプレゼントしてくださったこともありました。 そういう意味でも、堤先生は私にとって特別な存在です。 ジャンルが違うと思いすぎずに新しい出会いを楽しむ 22. 今後一緒に演奏してみたい音楽家を一人挙げるとしたら、誰ですか？ 新倉 まだ存じ上げていない方との出会いがある気がしているので、そういう方との出会いを楽しみにしたいです。今この時点で、あえて1人挙げるとしたら、ダニエル・ゼペックさんです。 バーゼルに留学中に室内楽の授業を受けたのですが、一緒に演奏すると学べることがあると思います。ゼペックさんのベートーヴェンの音楽にも感銘を受けたので、一緒に室内楽を弾いてみたいです。 ダニエル・ゼペックによるベートーヴェン：ピアノ三重奏曲 23. ジャンルを越えた活動にも取り組まれていますが、新しい音楽に出会うときに大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 結局、あまり「ジャンルが違う」と考えすぎないことだと思っています。自分が知らないことは、同じジャンルの中にもまだまだありますから。 新しい音楽に惹かれるときも、音楽そのものというより、「なぜこの魅力的な人は、この音楽を取り入れているんだろう」というところから興味を持つことが多いですね。 クレズマーなど東ヨーロッパの音楽に没頭していったのも、プロとアマチュアが一緒に演奏するバンドに入ったことがきっかけでした。音楽の響きはもちろんですが、そういう人たちに感動していることが多いんだと思います。 24. 今、音楽家として一番知りたいこと、探求したいことは何ですか？ 新倉 今回ベートーヴェンに取り組むことで、ベートーヴェンの知られざる一面をたくさん発見できました。なので、今回の12月3日の公演でも、きっと皆さまも「あ、そうなんだ」というところが見つかると思います。「そういう曲を書いていたんだ」とか、「そういう一面があるんだ」と。そういった意味で、残された曲に関しては、書かれた背景や作曲家の人となりを探求したいと思います。 うつむくベートーヴェンを気にかけてあげる新倉さん 25. これから、どんな音楽家になっていきたいですか？ 新倉 私は有名な国際コンクールに入賞しているわけでもないのですが、それでも第一線の皆さんと一緒に音を出させていただく機会に恵まれてきました。 なので、これからの若い方々が何か挫折したときに「あ、こういう音楽家もいた」と思っていただけるような、何か一つの例になれたらいいのかなと思っています。 いろいろなキャリアや肩書きがなくても、「自分なりの道があるよ」と思っていただける存在になりたいなと思っているので、それをキープ・ゴーイングでいきたいです。 新倉瞳に50の質問！〈後編〉新倉瞳の人となりは9月30日公開予定！ ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 新倉瞳さんの出演情報 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央 ベートーヴェンの小径 日時： 2026年12月3日（木）19：00開演 会場： サントリーホール items.body: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. The title track establishes the EP’s sound through layers of synthesiser harmonies that gather pace but stop short of a conventional climax. “Streams and Storms” turns towards private reflection, while “The Quiet Chaos of Playing It Safe” holds onto its tension without seeking a dramatic release. “Etude No. 1” strips the music down again, bringing the record to a sombre close. As Njoku explains in the accompanying interview, his move away from language is connected to an interest in how music can communicate feelings before they have been organised into words. Grief, exhaustion and recovery remain unresolved, expressed through harmony, resonance, dynamics and space. Small harmonic changes assume greater significance within these sparse arrangements. This is no suite in four movements, with constrasting character and same key signature. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE is a protean EP that searches and digs inwards, taking unexpected turns without any desire to dazzle. There is no show-off moment, no virtuoso display demanding attention, nor any grand moment of portending grief; emotion remains understated and kept in check. The music is unafraid of intimacy, allowing sustained harmonies, shifts in density and silence to determine its course, leaving much of the experience behind these compositions unspoken. To help us put out the fire we reached out directly to Tony Njoku for an interview conducted via email. All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was a large-scale collaborative statement concerned with spiritual preparedness, cultural resistance and collective survival, while the Bloom releases increasingly embraced instrumental composition, chamber arrangements and themes of grief, memory and renewal. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels like a further step in that direction: intensely personal, largely wordless and driven by the need to work through difficult emotions rather than narrative. Do you see this EP as the culmination of a journey that began with those recent releases, or did it emerge from a fundamentally different place? I don’t think of it as a culmination so much as another point of arrival. Each project tends to emerge from whatever questions I’m living with at the time. All Our Knives… was very outward-facing. It was about community, about bringing different voices into conversation around ideas of resilience and collective memory. Bloom and the instrumental work that followed became quieter spaces where I could sit with loss, change and the slower work of transformation. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE came from an even more internal place. I wasn’t trying to tell a story or resolve anything. I was more interested in documenting a state of being and exorcising some pent-up feelings that were essentially causing me harm. The music became a way of staying present with difficult emotions rather than translating them into language. In that sense it feels connected to the recent releases, but I wasn’t consciously trying to complete a trilogy or close a chapter. It simply became the form those experiences needed. One of the recurring threads across recent works—from The Loops (Grief) and Looking For Light to the standalone single “Malaise”—is an engagement with emotional turbulence that is neither entirely despairing nor entirely hopeful. The title track of A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE speaks of moving through fire rather than escaping it. Has your understanding of grief, burnout and recovery changed over the course of these releases, and do you think this EP arrives at a different emotional destination than those earlier works? I think grief has become less about something to overcome and more about something you learn to live alongside. Earlier work probably carried a stronger desire to find resolution or to move towards the light. I don’t think I see it that way anymore. Recovery isn’t linear, and neither is burnout. There are moments of joy inside exhaustion and moments of uncertainty inside healing. The image of moving through fire rather than escaping it felt important because some experiences can’t be bypassed. They change you. The music on this EP isn’t trying to extinguish the fire; it’s trying to understand what remains after you’ve passed through it. If there’s hope here, it’s a quieter kind. It’s found in endurance, attention and the possibility of continuing to create despite everything. One of the striking aspects of All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was the way you brought together an extraordinary community of Black British voices—Tricky, GAIKA, Ghostpoet, Coby Sey, James Massiah, Space Afrika, Labi Junior and others—creating a record that felt simultaneously personal and collective. More broadly, your recent work has moved freely between songs, spoken-word collaborations, chamber-like compositions, ambient electronics and abstract instrumental forms. By contrast, A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels almost entirely self-contained, built around piano, synthesisers and extended instrumental pieces. After such a collaborative album, did the absence of other voices create a different kind of honesty or vulnerability? Collaboration has always been fundamental to my practice because it allows ideas to exist beyond my own perspective. All Our Knives… couldn’t have existed without those voices. The conversations between people were the point of the record. With this EP I found myself needing the opposite experience. I needed solitude, not because I wanted to withdraw from community, but because I needed to hear what was underneath all the noise. Working mostly alone meant there was nowhere to hide. Every hesitation, every silence, every decision belonged to me. That can feel vulnerable, but it can also be very freeing because you’re no longer trying to explain yourself through words or through other people’s interpretations. I also needed space to cry and I find that’s a hard thing for me to do in front of people, I let go of my masks the most in solitude. So it became a conversation with the instruments themselves. The piano, synthesizers and space all became collaborators in a different sense. You’ve described this EP as a collection of “raging exhalations, quiet revelations, subtle smirks of humility, laments and meditations.” Unlike many of your previous releases, there are no guest vocalists, no lyrics and no obvious narrative anchors. Did working without words feel liberating or exposing? And at this stage in your career, do you feel instrumental music has become just as capable as song of carrying the political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always been central to your work? Working without words was both liberating and exposing. Lyrics can sometimes direct people towards a particular meaning, whereas instrumental music leaves much more room for the listener’s own experience. That openness was something I wanted to embrace. I’ve become increasingly interested in what music communicates before language enters. Breath, texture, resonance, silence… these things carry meaning too. They can hold emotion in ways that words sometimes can’t. I don’t really separate instrumental music from song anymore. They’re just different ways of asking the same questions. The political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always interested me don’t disappear when language disappears. They become embodied differently. Sometimes a sustained note or a shift in harmony can express something that would become smaller if I tried to explain it. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. The post The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Black Sherif takes his own sound apart on SUN SHERIF, the six-track EP he released through Blacko Management and EMPIRE in early September. The Konongo-born singer and rapper calls it “a deconstruction of everything Black Sherif’s done sonically“, a method that gives him the obsession he says he needs when working through fifteen or twenty demos at a time. That sound took shape on the “First Sermon” and “Second Sermon” singles of 2021, Twi verses set over highlife melody and UK drill drums, and in 2022 “Kwaku the Traveller” carried it to number one on Apple Music in Ghana and Nigeria. Two albums followed, The Villain I Never Was in 2022 and Iron Boy in April 2025. The EP brings in the Ghanaian singer AratheJay on “Forever” and the Trinidadian production duo Full Blown on “Love Again”, and Sherif sings “Jolie” alone, moving between Twi and English towards a chorus built on the French word for pretty. The verses are made of small acts of devotion: a New Year’s drive to her door, songs written for her in the manner of Kurt Cobain, a habit dropped because she disliked it. items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comAn outstanding album. The Chilean ensemble Asceta has established itself as one of those collectives you simply have to know if you are a fan of music made with extraordinary care and musicianship. Guided by the creative spirit of Rodrigo Maccioni, the band delivers an album in 2026 that, although there are still several months left in the year, could very well be considered the best Rock in Opposition and avant-prog release of the year. "The Fool Leading The Blind" is the title of the Chileans' third full-length release, an ambitious album that, across fifty three minutes, offers five compositions in which magic, social criticism, and music of the highest caliber take center stage. Everything begins with the album's title track, a twenty one minute suite that can be ominous at times, frenetic at others, and remarkably calm in between. The first three minutes are somewhat contemplative, as something gradually begins to take shape. Strings and drums establish a semi-slow rhythm that slowly builds until, around the four minute mark, the first explosion of rock arrives. Rock in Opposition, indeed, because the criticism directed toward our world and our politics is implicit throughout the piece, and the musicians express it through their constantly shifting yet remarkably intelligent way of communicating. I love the unexpected rhythmic changes, the moments when the energy and pulse suddenly rise, and the way every instrument introduces its own notes and ideas before converging into an incredibly solid composition that eventually leads us toward ecstasy. There is something beautiful about the way these musicians organize themselves to construct their music. I only wish that, as a society, we could demonstrate this same kind of organization when it comes to confronting bad governments and defending our land. After this emotional roller coaster, Asceta offers us the somber "Temple of Mirrors". Its opening minute is somewhat dissonant, with scattered sounds appearing here and there without any clearly defined form. Then, little by little, a structure begins to emerge, bringing clearer sounds and direction. Progressive music, naturally, but also classical music, an endless palette of colors and textures, and a remarkable convergence between acoustic and electric elements, as beautifully demonstrated by the guitar. Strings introduce the creepy and ominous atmosphere of "When They Arrive". Gradually, instruments such as bassoon, drums, and clarinet join the landscape, creating a dark environment in which a sense of unease comes naturally. There are brief bursts of intensity that could easily startle an unsuspecting listener, but there are also moments of harmony in which we can look around and decide which path to take. This is highly visual music, and every listen can inspire completely different stories in the listener's mind. There are passages that evoke After Crying or Art Zoyd. Wonderful. With "Everything Stopped", a frenetic and semi-chaotic rhythm takes over, constantly contrasted by pauses filled with cadence but also nervous energy. The ensemble creates fascinating musical connections. At times the strings take the spotlight, at others the winds or the drums, yet there is always a beautiful cohesion that serves as the thread connecting their performances. The music here is never linear, and that may initially turn away listeners who are not comfortable with such an approach. But once you connect with it, a genuine synergy develops, and it remains intact until the very end of the album. Speaking of endings, this magnificent record concludes with "Memento Mori", a ten minute composition that is colorful and multifaceted, filled with playful changes that bring brightness while contrasting beautifully with darker passages. The bass establishes an ongoing conversation with the clarinet and oboe, and as usual, the Chileans deliver a dose of avant-garde music of the highest caliber, something no fan of this particular musical territory should overlook. A well deserved round of applause for Asceta, lovers of art and natural opposers by conviction. May their talent and passion continue to drive them toward creating music as rewarding as this.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 988Tangerine Dream is a progressive electronic rock band that was founded in Berlin, Germany in 1967 by Edgar Froese, Klaus Schulze and Conrad Schnitzler. The band was among the earlier explorers of a new musical universe opened by electronic instruments. Tangerine Dream's music was born as a psychedelic journey in the heavens, and, aided by the new electronic keyboards, the band transformed into a contemplative survey of the universe. By borrowing from the impressionistic painting, (notably of Salvador Dali), the ecclesiastic music, the minimalist avant-garde, and the Eastern transcendental philosophy, Tangerine Dream invented "kosmische music", one of the most influential musical genres.Tangerine Dream released their debut studio work "Electronic Meditation" in 1970 with Froese, Schulze and Schnitzler. Still, "Electronic Meditation" isn't properly an electronic album. It consists mainly of experimental noises performed with classic rock instruments. So, it's more a rock album made with rock instruments. Actually it's a krautrock album, the musical style invented by the German musicians in the late of the 60's and early of the 70's. It was only on their second album "Alpha Centauri" that the synthesizers came into play. After the release of "Electronic Meditation", each member went his own separate way. The only member that remained in Tangerine Dream was Froese. With Froese, Christopher Franke and Steve Schroyder on the line up, the band released their second work "Alpha Centauri"."Alpha Centauri" is the second album of Tangerine Dream, released in 1971. The line up is Edgar Froese (voice, guitar, bass, organ, Fx and Mellotron), Steve Schroyder (voice, Hammond & Farfisa organs, electronics and percussion) and Christopher Franke (flute, piano, harp, zither, VCS 3 synthesizer, drums and percussion). "Alpha Centauri" also had the participation of Udo Dennenberg (voice and flute), Roland Paulick (VCS 3 synthesizer) and Peter Baumann (organ).As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is the first really electronic progressive rock album released by the band and where we can see for the first time the use of synthesizers by Tangerine Dream. The line up on the album consisted of a guitarist, a percussionist, a flutist and three keyboardists recording the three improvised jams of "Alpha Centauri" that defined the genre. Here, we can also see the presence, for the first time, of what is considered the best line up of the band, Froese, Franke and Baumann, despite the latter only appearing as guest. As happened with their debut work, "Alpha Centauri" became the only album with this official line up, Froese, Franke and Schroyder. And it became also tremendously closer to what Tangerine Dream would be all about than what their debut had been. Sure, it still sounded rather primitive and low-budget, but Tangerine Dream had now clearly discovered that spacey, atmospheric and dreamy experimental electronic music was the way to go for them. It would be completely proven with their next album "Zeit"."Alpha Centauri" has three tracks. "Sunrise In The Third System" contains some slow spacey sounds and effects. It's a stealthy and hypnotic piece, with a dense organ and a ghostly flute. It has a clear nod to Pink Floyd thanks to the sound of the organ. It forms a perfect introduction to the main cosmic journey, a kind of decompression chamber that helps the listener get acclimated to the alien landscape of Tangerine Dream's musical world. "Fly And Collision Of Comas Sola" slowly builds a heroic theme that eventually crashes into chaos. The track starts with a synthesizer and an organ in the background. The organ makes its appearance to establish the mattress on which flutes and synths build enveloping and disturbing sounds. As the song progresses, the drums appear closing with an abrupt ending. It allows us to envision great things in the future band's history. The title track is the centre piece of the album. It's an interesting improvisation based around spacey electronic sounds, organs and Froese's guitar. At the end goes into a poem spoken in German and climaxes into one of the few cases of human vocal-harmonies on a band's album. The flute makes a fine atmospheric contrast. It's an incredible spacey and timeless experience. You got the impression of leaving this world. It paves way for everything on their next album "Zeit" to all their famous lengthy epics like the title track on "Phaedra".Conclusion: As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is considered as the first electronic space album. It marks the transition from the krautrock to the electronic bubbling sound of their albums "Zeit" and "Atem" in their Pink phase. If "Electronic Meditation" had seemed better suited to a horror film, "Alpha Centauri" is firmly in the science fiction camp. The structure of the album would prove to be very representative for the several albums to come from the band, with one side long title track and a couple of "shorter" tracks on the other side. So, despite some technical shortcomings, "Alpha Centauri" was an important release in the musical evolution of Tangerine Dream. The mysterious cover painting and art design, by Edgar Froese and his wife at the time, Monique Froese, contribute directly to the album's character. As products of the psych era, "Alpha Centauri", "Zeit" and "Atem", are fine nuggets, even if the best was yet to come.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many factors at play with this soundtrack. First of all, it is worth noting that soundtracks often inspire great electronic music albums, given the genre's inherently cinematic and atmospheric nature, as seen with Klaus Schulze's Body Love. Edgar Froese, his bandmate in Tangerine Dream, turned the score for Wolf Gremm's film into his own sixth solo album. The movie also marked the final screen appearance of the German director Rainer Werner Fassbinder as an actor. Based on the novel Murder on the 31st Floor by Per Wahl��, the story is set in a future Germany where a private corporation holds power and all societal problems appear to have been solved, until a group calling itself "Kamikaze" issues a bomb threat. Detective Jansen (Fassbinder), clad in his signature leopard-print suit, then uncovers unexpected and deeply sinister connections and mysteries. The track "Videophonic" immediately immerses the listener in a sci-fi atmosphere; the music transcends standard synthesizer-based electronics, evoking the mysterious, perilous vibe of Krautrock."Vitamin C" is almost danceable, yet driven by a magnetic, funky groove; beneath the main rhythm lies a synthesizer wash that adds a progressive sheen, allowing the track to build, shift, evolve, and unfold organically. "Krismopompas" reminded me of Air, even though this album predates them, featuring dissonant notes; while knowing the film's plot helps, the track stands perfectly well on its own thanks to its strong melodic content. "Police Disco" shows traces of Vangelis but possesses an restless quality that lends it extreme dynamism; subtle classical influences lurk in the background, and there are echoes of Pink Floyd, specifically the Echoes era, giving the album an experimental edge that makes it compelling.With its electronic percussion, Police Therapy Center feels more rooted in the 80s; yet, there are underlying keyboard layers, like out-of-tune violins, providing subtle accompaniment, while the style shifts instantly to a highly martial funeral march on "Blue Panther." "Unexpected Death" is almost psychedelic, a realm where electronics also lend themselves well, acting as a malleable, mutating substance.Flying Kamikaze is ambient music with a spacey, ethereal vibe, reminiscent of Popol Vuh's work on Fitzcarraldo. Yet it is dark and mysterious, reflecting both the natural world and the ominous Berlin of this dark utopia. "Tower Block" conveys that feverish, concrete-laden urban atmosphere translated into music, while the closing track "The 31st Floor", which alludes to the original novel, broadens the horizon; blending electronica with the futuristic Krautrock style of Can's "Spoon" (from Ege Bamyasi) and straddling the line between film noir and dystopian sci-fi, Kamikaze 1989 showcased many of Froese's great strengths as a composer dedicated to illustrating mental imagery while maintaining his artistic independence.

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Wish You Were Here is one of those albums that does not need to be excessively complex to feel progressive. Released in 1975, it combines progressive rock, psychedelic rock, art rock and space rock into an incredibly cohesive and atmospheric experience. I would not consider it one of Pink Floyd's most overtly progressive albums, but its careful compositions, long instrumental developments, experimental production and thematic coherence make it a very strong progressive rock work.The atmosphere is probably the album's greatest strength. It is contemplative, melancholic, emotional and, at times, almost intellectual in the way its themes are presented. The production has aged remarkably well, with every instrument occupying its own space in the mix. The synthesizers and keyboards of Richard Wright are particularly impressive, adding an essential dimension to the album's sound.The centerpiece is undoubtedly "Shine On You Crazy Diamond", which I consider a masterpiece in its own right. I prefer to experience its different sections as one complete work rather than treating them as separate pieces. The song contains excellent instrumental development, especially in the guitars, drums and synthesizers. David Gilmour's guitar work is outstanding, combining technical ability with an enormous amount of emotional expression. Wright's keyboards are equally important, creating much of the psychedelic and spacious atmosphere that defines the piece.The emotional weight of "Shine On You Crazy Diamond" is also increased by its connection to Syd Barrett, whose work with Pink Floyd I greatly admire. Knowing that the song was written as a tribute to him gives the piece an additional emotional dimension. The feeling of loss and nostalgia is deeply present without overwhelming the music itself."Welcome to the Machine" is another major highlight. Its synthesizer work is simply magnificent, and the electronic textures create an almost mechanical atmosphere that perfectly complements the song's subject matter. The composition is less progressive in a traditional structural sense, but its sound design and atmosphere are remarkably creative. I would give the synthesizers an almost absurd 10/10 ? or, jokingly, 1,000,000/10. This is one of the clearest examples of how Pink Floyd could use studio production itself as part of the composition.The lyrics also contribute considerably to the album's thematic unity. Alongside the tribute to Syd Barrett, the record deals with the music industry and the way it can become destructive and dehumanizing. "Welcome to the Machine" and "Have a Cigar" are particularly effective in this regard. Even though these themes were written in the 1970s, they remain strikingly relevant today."Have a Cigar" is another very enjoyable track. Roy Harper's vocals work surprisingly well and have some similarities to Roger Waters' voice. The song is more accessible than some of the album's other material, but it still fits naturally into the overall concept.The title track, "Wish You Were Here", is probably the most commercially accessible song on the album. I personally rate it slightly below the other tracks, at 7/10, but it still serves an important role in the album as a whole. Its lyrics and emotional character provide another perspective on the themes of absence, loss and alienation.One of the things I appreciate most about Wish You Were Here is how naturally the tracks connect to each other. The album can almost feel like one long composition, rather than simply a collection of individual songs. The transitions, recurring atmosphere and production choices create an unusually strong sense of unity.From a progressive perspective, I would describe the album as moderately progressive. It is not constantly concerned with complex time signatures, virtuosity or extremely elaborate structures. Instead, its progressive qualities come from the development of ideas, extended instrumental passages, experimentation with sound, thematic coherence and the willingness to let atmosphere become a fundamental part of the composition.The instrumentation is excellent throughout. Gilmour's guitars are a major highlight, Wright's keyboards and synthesizers are perhaps the most distinctive element of the album for me, Nick Mason's drumming contributes effectively to the long developments, and the saxophone adds another color to the sound. The engineering and production are also outstanding, particularly in the way the instruments and effects are separated and integrated into the overall soundscape.The album's strongest qualities are "Shine On You Crazy Diamond," Richard Wright's synthesizers and keyboards, and David Gilmour's guitars and vocals. I honestly don't have any significant weaknesses to point out. Even though "Wish You Were Here" itself is the most commercial track and the one I personally rate lowest, it is still an important part of the complete experience.Overall, Wish You Were Here is an album in which you can become completely absorbed in the atmosphere of the music. It is contemplative, melancholic, psychedelic and emotionally powerful, while remaining carefully composed and remarkably cohesive.Alongside Meddle and Atom Heart Mother, it is among my favorite Pink Floyd albums.Essential for anyone interested in atmospheric and psychedelic progressive rock.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — The surname Gildenl'w is by no means unfamiliar to us. There's no need to explain why here. But it might be worth dwelling a bit on his first name. Born in Sweden, Kristoffer was the bassist for Pain of Salvation up until the double album *Be* (2004), and like most bassists, his demeanor was more low-key at the time, and his role seemingly less prominent than that of his brother, the frontman. Can we then speak of emancipation? Or simply of a search for another form of personal fulfillment? In any case, in 2003, at the height of the famous progressive metal band's popularity, Kristoffer left Sweden and Pain of Salvation to move to the Netherlands, collaborating on both sides of the Atlantic with some heavyweights of the progressive rock scene (Damien Wilson, Neal Morse, Lana Lane, the band Kayak'), before launching a solo career in 2012 with the album *Rust*.Begun in 2019 (alongside the album *Homebound*), *Empty*, Kristoffer Gildenl'w's fifth and latest solo album, was originally scheduled for 2020, but a devastating pandemic had other plans, and an unexpected *Let Me Be A Ghost* took precedence, releasing in 2021. Despite its overarching theme (depression), the album *Let Me Be A Ghost* still contained beautiful moments of musical serenity, a touch of melodic and harmonic lightness, as if weightless. There was gravity, too, but it knew how to be playful at times. And this ghostly imprint ultimately led to a kind of peace. 'Let Me Be A Ghost' seemed to describe the sensation of falling'but a fall from which one gets back up, with difficulty, not without effort, yet with courage and the feeling of having grown.'Empty' is even more striking because it offers a broader critical perspective on another tragic fall'that of humanity, drawn into the emptiness of our existence. The music thus becomes the anxious echo of a palpable despair that conveys the state of mind of a man struggling not to fall into this void'this vast, searing void that weighs on our hearts, terrified at the thought of what humanity is doing, a lost humanity in search of meaning.Like his previous solo albums, *Empty* possesses the same strange power of attraction'an irresistible pull that draws us entirely into a universe poised between dream and reality, between soothing light and revealing darkness. How can one resist lyrics so beautiful, so poignant'all these words that soar directly toward the heavens, sung in that deep, comforting, instantly recognizable voice that speaks of disarray, doubt, the pain of incomprehension in the face of human beings' self-destructive recklessness'a voice that speaks to us of our fears and sufferings as fragile beings, just as one might speak to a damned soul waiting in vain for its due.Despite all, one senses the presence of a mystery'a reflection on our purpose in life'carried by Kristoffer Gildenl'w's music and the brilliant artists who perform it. Each composition is a bewildering showcase of beauty, set to restrained vocals, but that is precisely what makes Kristoffer's style so powerful and heightens the emotional vertigo it evokes in us. Each track on his album is a profound and expansive anthem that can help us endure all the torments of the world. We can sense echoes of his former band. We can sense his love for Joni Mitchell, Mike Oldfield, and other giants of the '70s. We hear echoes of Anathema or Dire Straits. We encounter heart-wrenching blues ' la Pink Floyd, the kind whose mysteries were known only to Gilmour and Waters when they were still able to get along. It is dark and dense music, yet it regularly lightens, expands, shakes itself free, moves, and brightens'notably thanks to the graceful arabesques of Ben Mathot and Anne Bakker's violins, a rhythm section capable of softening its touch, the enchanting piano arpeggios played by Kristoffer himself, or the memorable feverish surges of the electric guitar tamed by sorcerers who seem to command the waves and the flames; all these warm notes like so many stars burning eternally to soothe our nights.*Empty* is one of those rich and profound progressive rock works that give us all the more the more we bring of ourselves to them as we receive them'intuitively felt by the heart yet always surprising to the ear. By giving us the best of himself here'which requires great courage' Kristoffer Gildenl'w sets an example by casting an intense light into the night of our troubled souls, illuminating with irrepressible hope a reality before which the malevolent structures of our destructive imagination and our death-dealing impulses dissolve'the only true light, the one that seeks to purify us of our unforgivable sins committed against Mother Nature. In the end, 'Empty' is neither sad nor despairing. In any case, even in the face of impending disaster, there will always be something good to take away'if only a tiny drop of happiness or a pinch of love.

items.body: Cold Spring releases SATØRI’s “Your Life Is Worth Nothing” on 2 October 2026, on CD in a matt-laminate digipak under catalog number CSR364CD. The album mixes harsh industrial noise and power electronics with hard, heavy beats, hostile vocals and dark electronics, and is priced at £9.49 in advance, rising to £11.49 after release. SATØRI’s eleven tracks on ‘Your Life Is Worth Nothing’ The album runs eleven tracks, recorded and mixed by Dave Kirby at Digitalis in Somerset across 2025 and 2026, mastered by Martin Bowes at The Cage Studios, with artwork by Abby Helasdottir: “Last Rites” (3:58) “Perverseverence” (3:47) “Don’t Bend: Break” (4:38) “Suck Out The Light” (3:52) “Seeds Of Darkness” (7:44) “Growing Violence” (6:09) “Trajan” (3:49) “Shattered” (3:52) “Haunted” (4:46) “Pillars Of Salt” (4:47) “Can’t Stop The Itch” (6:30) Track ten shares its title with SATØRI’s previous Cold Spring album, “Pillars Of Salt”, released in 2025. Your Life Is Worth Nothing by Satøri SATØRI described the album’s themes directly: “They think it. Sometimes you think it. A black oppression that takes over; consuming your very soul. The pointlessness of existence. Your single-minded fight against a world and what seems to be an entire population who invalidate everything you believe or stand for, create a climate in which you struggle to survive and destroy the opportunities for you to ever fulfil your potential. Remember: your life is worth nothing.” SATØRI live dates 2026 03.10.2026 – Glossop, UK – The Globe – album launch, with T.A.G.C. (Adi Newton of Clock DVA), Colossloth and Llyn Y Cwn 07.11.2026 – Barnstaple, UK – St Anne’s – with Colossloth and A Waste Of Damnation Side-Line has previously covered the Glossop date, where the album launch sits alongside Colossloth’s own new-album show and a T.A.G.C. set from Adi Newton. About SATØRI SATØRI formed in Margate, Kent, in 1984, when Dave Kirby and Robert Maycock began recording as Psychopath, adopting the name Satori in 1987, the same year Cold Spring-affiliated label Broken Flag released the project’s self-titled cassette. Further tapes followed on Mindscan Tapes through the late 1980s and into the early 1990s, including “Behold The Past”, “Power Of The Gun” and the “Techno Primitive” release credited to Satori Soundsystem. Maycock left in late 1993, Justin Mitchell joined in 1994, and the band disbanded in 1996. Mitchell revived Satori in 2006 with Neil Chaney, and the pair toured Japan alongside Sutcliffe Jugend in April 2007. Cold Spring picked up the project in 2008, releasing the album “Contemptus Mundi” and the CD edition of “Kanashibari” (its LP version had appeared in Japan on Dogma Chase earlier that year), alongside a split release with Merzbow and Sutcliffe Jügend and another with Nadja and Atavist. Dave Kirby, the sole constant member since 1987, resumed the project alone in 2014 and later began spelling the name SATØRI. Cold Spring has released two SATØRI albums under that spelling before the new record: “The Woods” in 2023 and “Pillars Of Salt” in 2025, making “Your Life Is Worth Nothing” the label’s third SATØRI album since Kirby’s solo return. The launch show for the new record takes place on 3 October 2026 at The Globe in Glossop, alongside album launches from Colossloth and a T.A.G.C. set from Adi Newton.

items.body: SAVAK releases “Door Deals And Debt: An Essential Collection From The First 10 Years” on October 23 via Peculiar Works, alongside Ernest Jenning Record Co. The 14-track compilation gathers material from the Brooklyn post-punk band’s first ten years together, drawing on the catalog built across its seven studio albums to date. The tracklist mixes familiar songs with deeper cuts rather than following a straight singles-only format. Eli Kasan of the Pittsburgh band The Gotobeds wrote the liner notes for the collection and was asked to help pick the tracklist; by his own account on the Bandcamp page, only four of his suggestions made the final cut. Kasan sums up the band’s decade-long run by writing that it amounts to “a decade in and no end in sight.” SAVAK’s ‘Door Deals And Debt’ tracklist The 14 songs on “Door Deals And Debt: An Essential Collection From The First 10 Years” are “Vis-a-Vis,” “No Blues No Jazz,” “Dead Dick,” “How Many Duchesses,” “Reaction,” “Like Gary Wilson Said,” “Paid Disappearance,” “Early Western Traders,” “No Man’s Island,” “Two Lamps,” “Sick Of War,” “Nature Erased,” “Empathy” and “Tomorrow And The Day After.” Door Deals And Debt: An Essential Collection From The First 10 Years by SAVAK SAVAK’s autumn tour dates SAVAK marks the release with a free record release show at Mama Tried in Brooklyn on October 25, then crosses to the UK for a run of November dates: October 25 – Brooklyn, NY – Mama Tried (record release show) October 29 – Norwich, UK – The Holloway October 30 – Newcastle, UK – The Lubber Fiend October 31 – Halifax, UK – Dukes November 1 – Nottingham, UK – The Old Cold Store (JT Soar Fest) November 2 – Oxford, UK – The Library November 3 – Bristol, UK – The Golden Lion November 4 – Birmingham, UK – Centrala November 5 – London, UK – The Old Blue Last November 6 – UK (venue TBA) November 7 – Sheffield, UK – CADS About SAVAK SAVAK formed in Brooklyn in 2015 around guitarists and singers Sohrab Habibion, previously of Obits and Edsel, and Michael Jaworski, previously of The Cops and Virgin Islands. Habibion and Jaworski split songwriting and lead vocals between them. Drummer Matt Schulz, also known for his work with Holy Fuck and Enon, rounds out the band’s current lineup; past lineups have included James Canty, Greg Simpson and Benjamin Van Dyke. The band released its debut album, “Best of Luck in Future Endeavors,” on Comedy Minus One in May 2016. It moved to Ernest Jenning Record Co. for “Cut-Ups” in 2017 and “Beg Your Pardon” in 2018, followed by the 12-inch single “Mirror Maker” in 2019, “Rotting Teeth in the Horse’s Mouth” in 2020, “Human Error / Human Delight” in 2022 and “Flavors of Paradise” in 2024, the latter two co-released with the band’s own label, Peculiar Works. Its seventh album, “SQUAWK!,” followed on May 30, 2025, ten years after the band’s first show. “Door Deals And Debt: An Essential Collection From The First 10 Years,” out October 23, 2026 via Peculiar Works and Ernest Jenning Record Co., draws its tracklist from across that decade.
